body: Fisher (Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits, 1958, ch.2): build a cross-section of opinions from competitors, customers, suppliers, ex-employees, researchers and trade-association staff; the composite picture of relative strength is surprisingly accurate. Buffett (1964): after the Nov-1963 salad-oil fraud hit American Express, he watched the cashier at Ross's Steak House in Omaha to see whether diners still used Amex cards and checked traveler's-cheque usage. Concluding the franchise was intact, he put about 40% of the partnership (about $13M) into the stock. The question was one decisive point (is the moat damaged?), not next quarter's EPS. Lynch: notice it first as a customer (Hanes L'eggs), and pass the two-minute drill. Question bank. Dealers: who is gaining counter share, what are the margins and credit terms, inventory days now versus 6 months ago, is stock being pushed at quarter-end. B2B customers: why this vendor over the L1 bidder, switching cost, wallet-share trend. Suppliers: does the company pay on time, has it asked for longer credit (an early stress sign). Ex-employees: culture, the promoter's treatment of minority money, capex discipline. Competitors: who prices irrationally, who is losing people. Records: state pollution-board consent-to-establish/operate (independently confirms capex timelines), MCA charges, eCourts, job postings, satellite imagery, app-store ratings. Keep a dated log.
title: Scuttlebutt for an individual investor in India: sources and question bank
